sub: Database system concepts, architecture, interfaces and data independence
def: A DBMS is a layered software system that stores a self-describing collection of data and insulates programs from it via the ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture, whose external, conceptual and internal levels buy logical and physical data independence.
exp:
The reason a DBMS exists at all is that file processing hard-codes structure into every program: the record layout lives in the application, so a changed field breaks every program that touches the file. A DBMS breaks that coupling by being self-describing — the description of the data lives inside the database itself, in the system catalog (also called the data dictionary), and the catalog's contents are metadata. MPSC has asked this twice with the two words swapped between the stem and the options, so hold both: what is stored is metadata, and the catalog or dictionary is where the DBMS stores it. In SQL systems the catalog is itself queryable as relations (INFORMATION_SCHEMA, pg_catalog, Oracle's data dictionary views), which is the practical proof that the description is data.

ANSI/SPARC defines three levels. The internal (physical) schema says how bytes are laid out — file organisation, page size, which indexes exist, clustering, compression. The conceptual (logical) schema is the community view: all entities, attributes, relationships and integrity constraints for the whole enterprise, with no storage detail. The external level is a set of user views, each showing one user group a slice of the conceptual schema. A query against a view is answered by two mappings, external-to-conceptual and conceptual-to-internal, and it is those mappings that the DBMS rewrites when a schema changes. That is exactly why the frequently asked contrast holds: logical design concerns the data itself, physical design concerns data types, storage and access paths.

Data independence is the payoff and it comes in two grades. Physical data independence is the ability to change the internal schema — add a B+ tree index, switch from a heap to a hash file, move a tablespace — without touching the conceptual schema or any application. It is largely achieved in practice. Logical data independence is the ability to change the conceptual schema — add an attribute, split a relation, add a new entity type — without changing the external schemas or the application programs written against them. It is much harder, and only survives changes that a view definition can absorb: if you vertically decompose Employee into two relations you can rebuild the old external view as a join, but if you drop an attribute the view that projected it cannot be saved. The exam wording to memorise is the mirror pair: logical data independence is immunity to changes in the logical (conceptual) structure; physical data independence is immunity to changes in the physical structure.

Schema versus instance is the same distinction on the time axis. The schema is the design, declared once by DDL and changed rarely; the instance (also called the database state, snapshot, or occurrence) is the set of rows present at one instant and changes with every committed transaction. The DBMS validates every state against the schema's constraints. Languages split along the same seam: DDL declares and alters structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML queries and changes data (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), with SDL/VDL for the internal and external levels in the classical account and DCL/TCL (GRANT, REVOKE, COMMIT, ROLLBACK) as the SQL additions. Interfaces run from menu- and form-based and natural-language front ends, through report generators and the DBA's own utilities (load, backup, reorganisation, performance monitoring), to embedded and dynamic SQL where the impedance mismatch between set-at-a-time SQL and record-at-a-time host code is bridged by a cursor. Three-tier client-server splits presentation, application logic and the database engine so the middle tier can pool connections and enforce business rules.

Roles are exam fodder because they overlap in real life but not on the paper. The DBA authorises access, tunes and designs the physical schema, plans backup and recovery, and is accountable for availability; the database designer chooses the conceptual schema from user requirements; the end user queries. Application programming is not a DBA duty, and neither is network management — MPSC has asked precisely that, with 'designing the physical schema' as the correct option against three distractors that are somebody else's job. Exam shape: this leaf is almost all MCQ, and almost all fill-in-the-blank pairs (schema/instance, logical/physical, catalog/metadata, DDL/DML). If it appears in the conventional half it will be 'explain the three-level architecture and how it achieves data independence' — draw the three boxes, name both mappings, and give one concrete change at each level that the layer above survives.
facts: The ANSI/SPARC architecture has three levels: external (user views), conceptual (community logical schema), and internal (physical storage), joined by two mappings.
Physical data independence is immunity to internal-schema change; logical data independence is immunity to conceptual-schema change, and is the harder of the two to achieve.
The system catalog (data dictionary) is where the DBMS stores its self-description; what it stores is called metadata.
A schema is the design and changes rarely; an instance (database state or snapshot) is the data present at one moment and changes with every update.
DDL declares structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP); DML manipulates data (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE); DCL grants and revokes privileges.
A cursor exists to resolve the impedance mismatch between SQL's set-at-a-time results and a host language's record-at-a-time processing.
Designing the physical schema, authorisation, backup and recovery planning, and performance tuning are DBA responsibilities; writing application code is not.
Program-data independence replaces file processing's practice of embedding the record structure in every application program.
traps: Catalog versus metadata: 'the data about relations that the system maintains' is metadata, but 'the place the system maintains it' is the catalog or data dictionary. MPSC has asked both phrasings with the other word as a distractor — read which noun the stem is asking for.

Logical versus physical data independence is defined by what you are protected FROM, not by which layer you sit in: logical data independence means changes in the logical structure do not reach the application. Options that say 'ability to modify the physical schema' describe the mechanism, not the definition.

Schema versus instance is often given in a blank-pair where the order is reversed in one option; the logical design is the schema and the point-in-time snapshot is the instance, never the other way round.

'Logical design focusses on the data itself, physical design on how it is stored and accessed' — a distractor pairing ER-diagram with SQL, or MySQL with Oracle, is naming tools rather than design levels.
mnem: Three levels, two independences: External-Conceptual-Internal, and you are independent of whatever level is BELOW you — logical independence sits above the conceptual level, physical independence above the internal one.

sub: Data models and the relational model: keys, tuples, domains and relational algebra
def: A data model is a set of concepts for describing structure, constraints and operations on data; the relational model represents the database as a set of relations, each a subset of the Cartesian product of the domains of its attributes, and manipulates them with relational algebra.
exp:
Codd's definition is the one the paper quotes almost verbatim, so hold it exactly. Each attribute A has a domain dom(A), the set of permitted atomic values for it. A relation schema R(A1,…,An) has degree n. A relation instance r is a subset of dom(A1) × dom(A2) × … × dom(An) — a subset of the Cartesian product of a list of domains, not of attributes, not of tuples. Its elements are tuples, and its cardinality is the number of them. Two consequences follow immediately and both are asked: because a relation is a set, tuples may be in any order and duplicate tuples cannot exist; and because domains are atomic, no attribute value may be a set or a repeating group, which is precisely what 1NF later restates. In relational-model terminology the correspondences are table = relation, row = tuple, column = attribute, column type = domain, table description = relation schema.

The key hierarchy is a chain of nested definitions and MPSC asks it four or five different ways. A superkey is any set of attributes whose values are unique across tuples — any set that functionally determines the whole record; the full attribute set is always a superkey. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: remove any attribute and uniqueness is lost. So the phrase 'minimal number of attributes needed to identify a record' selects candidate key, while 'a set of one or more attributes taken collectively to uniquely identify a record', with no minimality clause, selects super key. The primary key is the one candidate key the designer picks; the others become alternate keys. An attribute belonging to some candidate key is a prime attribute, which is the vocabulary 2NF and 3NF are stated in. A foreign key is an attribute set in one relation drawing its values from the primary key of another. If R(A,B,C,D,E) has the single candidate key A, then every superkey is A plus any subset of the remaining four attributes, so there are 2⁴ = 16 superkeys — a one-line count worth knowing.

The three constraint families are domain constraints (each value lies in dom(A)), entity integrity (no component of a primary key may be NULL, because a NULL cannot identify), and referential integrity: the values in the foreign-key attributes of the referencing relation must appear in the specified attributes of at least one tuple of the referenced relation, or be wholly NULL. That last sentence is close to the exam's own wording, and the maintenance options — ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, RESTRICT/NO ACTION — are what 'considered during design' means when a paper asks what you weigh when creating a foreign-key constraint.

Relational algebra is procedural: an expression says which operations to perform and in what order, and it is closed, so every operation returns a relation that another operation can consume. Tuple relational calculus and domain relational calculus are non-procedural — you state what you want, not how — and Codd's theorem says the algebra and the safe calculus have identical expressive power. There are six primitive operations: select σ (horizontal, row filter), project π (vertical, and it eliminates duplicates because the result is a set), union ∪, set difference −, Cartesian product ×, and rename ρ. Union and difference require union compatibility: same degree and pairwise compatible domains. Everything else is derived: intersection is R ∩ S = R − (R − S); the theta-join R ⋈θ S is σθ(R × S); the natural join equates all like-named attributes and then projects one copy away; the equi-join uses only equality predicates and keeps both copies. Cartesian product is the operation that pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S regardless of whether values match, giving |R| × |S| tuples — with 5,000 and 2,000 tuples that is 10,000,000, which is why an optimiser works so hard to turn a product plus a selection back into a join.

Division is the derived operator most often skipped and most often the hard MCQ. If Enrolled(sid, cid) holds (S1,C1), (S1,C2), (S1,C3), (S2,C1), (S2,C3), (S3,C2) and Required(cid) holds C1 and C2, then Enrolled ÷ Required = {S1}: S2 is missing C2 and S3 is missing C1. Division answers 'for all' queries, and expands to π_sid(Enrolled) − π_sid((π_sid(Enrolled) × Required) − Enrolled). Exam shape: this leaf is the densest MCQ leaf in the unit — fourteen bank questions, mostly one-line definitional stems on keys, domains and which language is procedural. In the conventional half it appears as 'write the following queries in relational algebra', where the marks go to using ÷ or a difference for the universal-quantifier query and to getting union compatibility right before you write ∪.
facts: A relation is a subset of the Cartesian product of a list of domains; its degree is the number of attributes and its cardinality the number of tuples.
A candidate key is a minimal superkey; a superkey need not be minimal, and the whole attribute set is always a superkey.
If a relation has n attributes and exactly one candidate key of k attributes, it has 2^(n−k) superkeys.
Relational algebra is procedural; tuple and domain relational calculus are non-procedural, and Codd's theorem makes the algebra and the safe calculus equally expressive.
The six primitive relational-algebra operations are σ, π, ∪, −, × and ρ; ∩, ⋈ and ÷ are derived, with R ∩ S = R − (R − S).
Union and set difference demand union compatibility: equal degree and pairwise compatible domains. Cartesian product and join do not.
Entity integrity forbids NULL in any component of a primary key; referential integrity requires foreign-key values to exist in the referenced relation or be entirely NULL.
Tuples of a relation have no inherent order and no duplicates, because a relation is a set; π therefore eliminates duplicates whereas SQL's SELECT does not.
traps: Super key versus candidate key hinges on one word: if the stem says 'minimal' or 'minimum number of attributes' the answer is candidate key, and if it merely says 'one or more attributes taken collectively to uniquely identify a record' the answer is super key. The bank contains both stems with the same option list.
'Subset of a Cartesian product of a list of ______' — the blank is domains, not attributes and not tuples. Attributes are names; the product is taken over their value sets.

Equi-join versus natural join: FROM A, B WHERE A.x = B.x is an equi-join and keeps both x columns, which is why the exam's sample SELECT lists CUSTOMER_T.CUSTOMER_ID and ORDER_T.CUSTOMER_ID separately. A natural join would have matched on name automatically and returned one copy.

A foreign key references the primary key (or a candidate key) of the other relation, never a super key or an arbitrary attribute — an option offering 'super key' is testing whether you know uniqueness alone is not enough.
mnem: Super ⊇ Candidate ⊇ Primary: dropping the word 'minimal' promotes candidate back up to super, and picking one candidate demotes it to primary.

def: The Entity-Relationship model is a high-level, implementation-independent semantic data model that describes a miniworld as entity types with attributes, relationship types among them, and constraints on cardinality and participation, and is the standard notation for conceptual database design before mapping to relations.
exp:
ER modelling sits at the conceptual level: it is deliberately free of tables, data types and indexes so that requirements can be argued with users before storage decisions harden. An entity is a thing with independent existence; an entity type is the schema-level description and an entity set is its current extension. The descriptive property every entity set possesses is an attribute — that exact phrasing appears in the bank, so keep 'attribute' attached to 'descriptive property'.

Attributes classify along four independent axes, and MPSC's questions come almost entirely from this taxonomy. Simple (atomic) versus composite: Address splits into Street, City, Pincode. Single-valued versus multi-valued: PhoneNumber can hold several values for one employee, which is the definition an option should give — an attribute that can have multiple values for a single entity instance, not one that depends on several other attributes. Stored versus derived: AGE computed from DATE_OF_BIRTH is derived, because its value is calculable from other stored data rather than kept independently; the exam has asked this both abstractly and with the AGE/DATE_OF_BIRTH pair. And key versus non-key. NULL covers the not-applicable and the unknown cases. In Chen notation an entity is a rectangle, a weak entity a double rectangle, a relationship a diamond, an identifying relationship a double diamond, an attribute an ellipse, multi-valued a double ellipse, derived a dashed ellipse, key attributes underlined, partial keys dash-underlined, and total participation a double line.

A relationship type's degree is the number of participating entity types — binary, ternary, or recursive when one entity type participates twice under two role names. Two constraints govern it. The cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N) caps how many relationship instances an entity may take part in; the participation constraint says whether every entity must participate (total, drawn as a double line, an existence dependency) or may not (partial). The alternative (min,max) notation folds both into one pair written on the line, where min = 1 means total participation. Counting is easy here and worth doing: between an entity set of m entities and one of n entities, an M:N relationship admits at most m × n instances, a 1:N relationship at most n, and a 1:1 relationship at most min(m,n).

A weak entity type has no attributes sufficient to form a primary key of its own; it is identified by a partial key (discriminator) combined with the primary key of its owner entity type, reached through an identifying relationship, and it always has total participation in that relationship. Dependent-of-an-employee is the canonical case. Be warned that two textbook traditions collide here and the bank contains a question that follows the second one: in Elmasri and Navathe a weak entity is by definition ID-dependent, whereas in Kroenke's terminology 'weak entity' means only existence-dependent, and 'ID-dependent entity' is the narrower kind whose identifier actually contains the parent's identifier. If a stem says 'cannot exist unless another entity exists, but does not require that the other entity's identifier be part of its own identifier', it is using the Kroenke split and wants 'weak entity'; if the stem is the plain 'lacks sufficient attributes to form a primary key', it wants weak entity too, under either tradition.

EER adds specialisation and generalisation (an IS-A hierarchy, with disjoint-versus-overlapping and total-versus-partial constraints, and attribute inheritance downward), aggregation for treating a relationship as an entity so another relationship can attach to it, and union/category types. Mapping to relations is the step that carries conventional marks, so learn the rules as counts. Each strong entity type becomes one relation. Each weak entity type becomes one relation whose primary key is owner PK plus partial key. Each multi-valued attribute becomes its own relation keyed on owner PK plus the attribute. A binary M:N relationship always becomes its own relation whose key is the union of the two participating primary keys, so two entities plus one M:N relationship yields three tables. A 1:N relationship needs no new table — post the 1-side's primary key as a foreign key into the N-side relation — so two entities plus one 1:N yields two tables. A 1:1 relationship folds into whichever side has total participation. A relationship's own descriptive attributes go into the relation that the relationship maps to, or into the N-side when it was folded. A ternary M:N:P relationship needs its own relation with all three keys.

Exam shape: the MCQs are definitional and land squarely on the attribute taxonomy and on weak entities. The conventional half is where this leaf pays — 'design an ER model for a university/hospital/transport department and map it to relational schemas' is a standard long-answer, and because the brief forbids diagrams here, practise stating the model in prose: entity types with their key attributes, then each relationship with its degree, cardinality ratio and participation, then the mapped table list with primary and foreign keys named. Marks are lost by forgetting total participation, by inventing a table for a 1:N relationship, and by leaving an M:N relationship without one.
facts: A derived attribute is calculated from other attributes rather than stored, as AGE is from DATE_OF_BIRTH; a multi-valued attribute holds several values for one entity instance.
A weak entity type lacks attributes sufficient to form its own primary key and is identified by its owner's primary key plus its own partial key (discriminator).
A weak entity always has total participation in its identifying relationship, drawn as a double line in Chen notation.
The degree of a relationship type is the number of participating entity types, not the number of entities involved.
A binary M:N relationship must map to its own relation, keyed on the union of both participating primary keys; a 1:N relationship maps by posting the 1-side key as a foreign key into the N-side.
Between entity sets of size m and n, an M:N relationship admits at most m × n instances, 1:N at most n, and 1:1 at most min(m, n).
In (min,max) notation, min = 1 states total participation and min = 0 states partial participation.
EER generalisation hierarchies carry two orthogonal constraints: disjoint versus overlapping, and total versus partial specialisation.
traps: Multi-valued versus composite versus derived: 'can have multiple values for a single entity instance' is multi-valued; 'decomposes into meaningful sub-parts' is composite; 'calculated from other attributes' is derived. An option reading 'depends on multiple other attributes' describes a functional dependency, not a multi-valued attribute.

Weak entity versus ID-dependent entity: Elmasri-Navathe treats them as the same thing, Kroenke does not. A stem that explicitly says the parent's identifier is NOT part of the child's identifier is using Kroenke's split and wants 'weak entity'; do not let 'ID-dependent entity' pull you across.
Cardinality ratio and participation are separate constraints. A 1:N relationship says nothing about whether participation is total, and marking a relationship 1:N does not make either side mandatory.

Business rules are declarative statements that may include restrictions and must be expressible as code or constraints; options claiming a business rule 'should be complex' or 'should not be convertible to computer code' invert the intent of the concept.
mnem: Attribute shapes as ellipse variants: one line simple, double line many values, dashed line derived (dashed = not really stored).

def: SQL is the declarative, non-procedural standard language of the relational DBMS, combining a data definition language for schema objects, a data manipulation language for querying and changing rows, and control sub-languages for privileges and transactions.
exp:
SQL is a query language, and the paper's own wording for it is that a query language is what most DBMSs give users for accessing data — not a 3GL, not a 4GL. Its sub-languages are the first thing to fix. DDL alters the database design: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, and it is DDL that defines the structure of a relation, deletes relations and relates schemas. DML manipulates the data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DCL is GRANT and REVOKE, TCL is COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT. Blank-pair questions almost always come down to DDL for structure versus DML for data.

The destructive verbs are easy marks and easy losses. DROP TABLE removes the relation itself, schema and rows together — that is the answer to 'remove a relation from an SQL database'. DELETE FROM removes tuples and can carry a WHERE clause. TRUNCATE removes every row as a DDL operation, usually without firing row triggers and usually not rollback-able in the way a DELETE is. To add an integrity constraint to a relation that already exists you use ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT, never CREATE TABLE and never a nonexistent 'MODIFY TABLE'.

The three DML statement shells are worth writing out because MPSC has asked each with one keyword blanked. UPDATE instructor SET salary = salary * 1.05 WHERE …; the keyword after the table name is SET, and omitting the WHERE clause updates every row. INSERT comes in two forms: INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (…) for a literal tuple, and INSERT INTO t SELECT … FROM other WHERE … for inserting tuples drawn from another relation — the SELECT form is the one an exam means by 'insert a tuple from another relation', and the column lists must be union-compatible in degree and type. DELETE with a correlated or nested condition uses a subquery, as in DELETE FROM instructor WHERE dept_name IN (SELECT dept_name FROM department WHERE building = 'MilleniumCenter'); note that the subquery must return the values being compared, so a bare string literal after IN, or deleting from the wrong table, are the standard wrong options.

Joins are the densest MCQ target. An inner join keeps only matching tuples and preserves no non-matched tuples on either side. A left outer join preserves the non-matched tuples of the left relation only, padding the right side with NULLs; a right outer join does the mirror; a full outer join preserves both. A natural join is an inner join that matches automatically on all like-named columns and returns one copy of each; an equi-join uses an explicit equality predicate and keeps both copies, which is why SELECT CUSTOMER_T.CUSTOMER_ID, ORDER_T.CUSTOMER_ID … FROM CUSTOMER_T, ORDER_T WHERE CUSTOMER_T.CUSTOMER_ID = ORDER_T.CUSTOMER_ID is an equi-join and not a natural join. A comma-separated FROM with no WHERE predicate is a Cartesian (cross) join. A self-join joins a table to an aliased copy of itself.

Grouping and NULLs supply the applied questions. The logical evaluation order is FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT and DISTINCT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT — which is why an alias defined in SELECT is unavailable in WHERE, and why a condition on an aggregate must go in HAVING while a condition on a raw column belongs in WHERE. NULL semantics follow three-valued logic and are counter-intuitive on purpose. On a column b holding 10, NULL, 10, NULL, COUNT(*) returns 4 but COUNT(b) returns 2, because every aggregate except COUNT(*) skips NULLs; SUM(b) is 20 and AVG(b) is 10, computed over two rows, not four. WHERE b <> 10 returns zero rows, not two, because NULL <> 10 evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE. And 5 NOT IN (SELECT b FROM t) returns nothing at all when b contains a NULL, since the comparison can never be proven true — the standard fix is NOT EXISTS, or filtering the NULLs out of the subquery. Only IS NULL and IS NOT NULL test for NULL.

Stored program objects close the leaf. A stored procedure is invoked explicitly by CALL or EXECUTE; a function returns a value and can be used inside an expression; a trigger is the special kind of stored procedure that is not called at all but fires as a side-effect of a data operation — INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE — on a table, with BEFORE/AFTER timing and ROW/STATEMENT granularity. Declarative referential action is preferable to a trigger where it suffices: ON DELETE CASCADE on the foreign key makes deleting a parent row delete the referencing child rows automatically, and ON DELETE SET NULL and ON UPDATE CASCADE are its siblings. A view is a stored query, updatable only in restricted cases, and the mechanism by which logical data independence is delivered. Exam shape: SQL is MCQ-heavy here, mostly single-keyword blanks and join-semantics stems, but the conventional half regularly asks you to write four or five queries against a given schema — aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING, a correlated subquery, and an outer join are the three that carry the marks.
facts: DROP TABLE removes the relation and its schema; DELETE removes tuples; TRUNCATE removes all rows as a DDL operation.
ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT is how an integrity constraint is added to an already existing relation.
The UPDATE statement's assignment clause keyword is SET; omitting WHERE updates every tuple in the relation.
INSERT INTO t SELECT ... FROM other is the form that inserts tuples drawn from another relation; INSERT ... VALUES inserts literals.
A left outer join preserves non-matched tuples of the left relation only; an inner join preserves non-matched tuples from neither side.
Every aggregate except COUNT(*) ignores NULLs: over the values 10, NULL, 10, NULL, COUNT(*) is 4, COUNT(b) is 2, SUM(b) is 20 and AVG(b) is 10.
A trigger is a stored procedure executed as a side-effect of an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table, rather than by explicit invocation.
ON DELETE CASCADE on a foreign key deletes the child rows that reference a deleted parent row, declaratively and without a trigger.
Clauses are evaluated FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT/DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — so WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups.
traps: NOT IN against a subquery that can return NULL yields no rows at all, because the comparison evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE; NOT EXISTS does not have this defect. Likewise WHERE col <> 10 silently excludes rows where col IS NULL.

Natural join versus equi-join: a query written as FROM A, B WHERE A.k = B.k is an equi-join — it retains both key columns and requires you to name the predicate. Natural join is implicit on like-named columns and projects one copy away.
CASCADE alone is not the answer to 'which clause deletes the child rows'; the clause is ON DELETE CASCADE, and CASCADE by itself also appears in DROP ... CASCADE with an entirely different meaning.

A trigger is a stored procedure but a stored procedure is not a trigger: the distinguishing phrase is 'executed as a side-effect' or 'in response to an action on the table'. If the stem says it is invoked by the application, it is a procedure or a function.
SQL's SELECT does not eliminate duplicates but relational algebra's π does — do not carry the algebra's set semantics into a SQL question unless DISTINCT is written.
mnem: DDL Defines, DML Manipulates, DCL Controls access, TCL Concludes the transaction.

sub: Database design, functional dependencies and normal forms
def: A functional dependency X → Y asserts that any two tuples agreeing on X must agree on Y; normalisation is the process of decomposing relation schemas so that every dependency is enforced by a key, progressing through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF and 4NF, and inclusion dependencies express that the projection of one relation is contained in the projection of another.
exp:
Redundancy is the disease and dependency is the diagnosis. If a relation stores a fact more than once, an update can change one copy and not the other, an insertion can be impossible until unrelated data exists, and a deletion can destroy information that was only incidentally stored there — the update, insertion and deletion anomalies. Every one of them traces back to a non-trivial functional dependency X → Y where X is not a key. Normalisation reduces redundancy and thereby protects data integrity; it does not improve readability and it does nothing for security, which is why the classic multiple-statement MCQ on 'what normalisation achieves' takes only the integrity and redundancy statements.

The computational core is the attribute closure X⁺: start with X and repeatedly add the right-hand side of any FD whose left-hand side is already inside, until nothing changes. X is a superkey iff X⁺ is the whole attribute set, and a candidate key iff additionally no proper subset of X has that property. Take R(A,B,C,D,E) with F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}. Then A⁺ = A, B, C, then D via B → D, then E via CD → E, giving ABCDE; E⁺ = E, A and thence all of ABCDE; BC⁺ = B, C, D, then E, then A, giving ABCDE; CD⁺ = C, D, E, A, B. But B⁺ = BD only and C⁺ = C only, so BC is minimal. The candidate keys are therefore A, E, BC and CD, the prime attributes are A, B, C, D and E — every attribute — and AB is a superkey but not a candidate key. Two shortcuts save time under exam conditions: an attribute that appears on the left of some FD and never on the right of any non-trivial FD must belong to every candidate key, and an attribute appearing on neither side must also be in every key. Applied to a relation whose only non-trivial dependencies are B → C, BC → A and E → A, the attributes B, D and E never occur on a non-trivial right-hand side, so the sole candidate key is BDE, and neither A, nor D, nor BC is a key on its own — which is exactly the reasoning an FD-and-key MCQ is testing even when its option list is imperfect.

Armstrong's axioms are sound and complete for FDs: reflexivity (Y ⊆ X implies X → Y), augmentation (X → Y implies XZ → YZ), transitivity (X → Y and Y → Z imply X → Z). Union, decomposition and pseudo-transitivity are derived. F⁺ is the closure of the FD set; a minimal (canonical) cover is an equivalent set with single attributes on the right, no redundant FD and no redundant left-hand attribute, and it is the input to 3NF synthesis.

The normal-form ladder, stated in the vocabulary that matters. 1NF: every attribute value is atomic — no repeating groups, no set-valued or composite attributes. 2NF: 1NF plus no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key, so a relation whose every candidate key is a single attribute is automatically in 2NF. 3NF: 2NF plus, for every non-trivial X → A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute — equivalently, no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on a key. BCNF: for every non-trivial X → A, X must be a superkey, with no prime-attribute escape hatch. 4NF: for every non-trivial multi-valued dependency X ↠ Y, X must be a superkey. A transitive dependency in exam shorthand is a functional dependency among non-key attributes.

Work the standard case. Empdt1(empcode, name, street, city, state, pincode), key empcode, with pincode → city, state and (street, city, state) → pincode. The only candidate key is a single attribute, so no partial dependency is possible and the relation is in 2NF. But empcode → pincode → city is a transitive dependency of the non-prime attribute city on the key, so 3NF fails: Empdt1 is in 2NF and hence 1NF, and no further. The fix is to split out Pincode(pincode, city, state) and leave Employee(empcode, name, street, pincode).

Now the case that separates 3NF from BCNF, which the exam loves precisely because the two coincide most of the time. Take R(A,B,C) with F = {AB → C, C → B}. AB⁺ = ABC and AC⁺ = ABC, so there are two overlapping candidate keys, AB and AC, and all three attributes are prime. The FD C → B does not violate 3NF, because its right-hand side B is a prime attribute — so R is in 3NF. It does violate BCNF, because C⁺ = BC is not the whole schema and C is therefore not a superkey. Decomposing on the violating dependency gives R1(C,B) and R2(A,C). That decomposition is lossless, since R1 ∩ R2 = {C} and C → B makes C a key of R1 — the binary lossless-join test is that the common attributes must functionally determine one of the two fragments. But it is not dependency-preserving: neither fragment can enforce AB → C, which is now only checkable by joining. State the trade-off honestly, because a conventional answer that omits it loses marks: a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into 3NF always exists and the synthesis algorithm from a minimal cover produces one, whereas BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may be forced to sacrifice dependency preservation. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF; the converse fails only when a violating determinant sits inside overlapping candidate keys, as above.

4NF handles the redundancy FDs cannot see. In Offering(course, instructor, textbook), where the instructors of a course and its prescribed textbooks are independent of one another, course ↠ instructor and course ↠ textbook hold, and a course with 2 instructors and 3 textbooks forces 6 tuples to record what is really 2 + 3 = 5 facts. There is no FD to blame — instructor does not determine textbook — yet the redundancy is real. Decomposing into (course, instructor) and (course, textbook) reaches 4NF, and a non-trivial MVD in a relation with only two attributes cannot exist, which is why 4NF is stable there.

Inclusion dependencies are the syllabus's named extension and are usually skipped. An inclusion dependency R[X] ⊆ S[Y] states that every projection of R onto X appears among the projections of S onto Y. Referential integrity is precisely the special case where Y is a key of S, so a foreign key is an inclusion dependency plus a key constraint. INDs also arise where FDs cannot express the requirement: an EER IS-A hierarchy mapped to tables yields Manager[empno] ⊆ Employee[empno], and an M:N relationship table yields one IND per participating entity. Their inference rules are reflexivity, projection with permutation, and transitivity; note that they are not Armstrong's axioms and that FDs and INDs do not interact simply — the combined implication problem is undecidable in general, which is the reason inclusion dependencies get their own normal-form theory rather than folding into the FD ladder. Exam shape: an MCQ will test one definition (transitive dependency, or which normal form a given schema reaches); the conventional half asks you to take a schema plus an FD set, find the candidate keys, name the highest normal form and decompose, and the marks live in showing the closure computation and in checking losslessness and dependency preservation of the result rather than just naming the fragments. Denormalisation, deliberately reintroducing redundancy for read performance, is a legitimate design decision at the physical level and worth one sentence in a long answer.
facts: X is a superkey iff X⁺ is the entire attribute set, and a candidate key iff no proper subset of X has that property.
For R(A,B,C,D,E) with A → BC, CD → E, B → D and E → A, the candidate keys are A, E, BC and CD.
An attribute that never appears on the right-hand side of any non-trivial FD must be contained in every candidate key.
2NF forbids partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on a candidate key, so a relation whose candidate keys are all single attributes is automatically in 2NF.
3NF allows a non-trivial X → A when A is a prime attribute; BCNF does not, requiring X to be a superkey in every case.
R(A,B,C) with AB → C and C → B is in 3NF but not BCNF, because its candidate keys AB and AC overlap and B is prime.
A binary decomposition is lossless iff the common attributes functionally determine at least one of the two fragments.
3NF synthesis from a minimal cover is always lossless and dependency-preserving; BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may fail to preserve dependencies.
4NF requires the left side of every non-trivial multi-valued dependency to be a superkey; a two-attribute relation admits no non-trivial MVD.
An inclusion dependency R[X] ⊆ S[Y] generalises referential integrity, which is the case where Y is a key of S; its inference rules are reflexivity, projection with permutation, and transitivity.
traps: 3NF versus BCNF: the ONLY difference is 3NF's prime-attribute exemption. If the determinant of a violating FD is a non-superkey but its right-hand side is part of some candidate key, the relation is in 3NF and not in BCNF — this needs overlapping candidate keys, so a schema with a single candidate key that is in 3NF is automatically in BCNF.
Do not assume a decomposition is dependency-preserving because it is lossless; the two properties are independent, and the standard BCNF example loses AB → C while remaining lossless.
Normalisation buys reduced redundancy and data integrity. It does not buy readability, and it does not buy security — a 'select all that apply' option list will offer both as decoys.

A candidate-key MCQ is answered by closure, not by inspection. Computing only some attributes' closures and stopping at the first that reaches the full schema can miss that a shorter subset also does, which changes minimality and therefore the answer.
Transitive dependency in exam usage means a functional dependency between non-key attributes, not merely any chained FD; a chain that ends at a prime attribute does not break 3NF.
mnem: Ladder in one line: 1NF atomic values, 2NF the whole key, 3NF nothing but the key, BCNF and nothing but the key even for prime attributes, 4NF and no independent multi-valued facts sharing a table.
rel: Data models and the relational model: keys, tuples, domains and relational algebra

def: Query processing is the sequence of parsing and translation, optimisation, and evaluation by which a DBMS turns a declarative SQL statement into an executable plan; optimisation chooses among equivalent relational-algebra expressions and among the physical algorithms implementing each operation, using heuristic transformation rules, catalogue statistics and cost estimates measured in block transfers and seeks.
exp:
SQL says what, not how, so something must supply the how. The parser produces a canonical relational-algebra expression — typically the naive one, a Cartesian product of every relation in the FROM clause with the whole WHERE predicate applied on top. The optimiser rewrites that tree into an equivalent but cheaper one and annotates each node with a physical algorithm, producing an evaluation plan; the evaluation engine executes it. Cost is dominated by disk I/O, so it is counted in block transfers plus disk seeks, with CPU cost usually ignored at exam level. The catalogue supplies the statistics the estimates need: n_r tuples in r, b_r blocks, f_r blocking factor, and V(A, r), the number of distinct values of attribute A in r.

Estimation rules follow from those statistics. An equality selection σ_{A=v}(r) is estimated at n_r / V(A,r) tuples, and at 1 if A is a key. A natural join r ⋈ s on a common attribute A is estimated at n_r × n_s / max(V(A,r), V(A,s)) tuples, and at most n_r tuples when A is a key of s, since each tuple of r then matches at most one tuple of s. These estimates are what make a cost-based optimiser's choices, and the reason bad statistics produce bad plans.

Join algorithm costs are where the calculation lives, so work a concrete pair. Let r hold 5,000 tuples in 100 blocks and s hold 2,000 tuples in 50 blocks, with neither fitting in the buffer and no index on either. Simple nested-loop join with r outer scans s once per tuple of r: n_r × b_s + b_r = 5,000 × 50 + 100 = 250,100 block transfers. Block nested-loop join scans s once per block of r instead: b_r × b_s + b_r = 100 × 50 + 100 = 5,100 — a factor of roughly fifty saved by nothing but changing the granularity of the outer loop. Because the product term b_r × b_s is symmetric, the tie-breaker is the additive term, so putting the smaller relation outside is marginally better: 50 × 100 + 50 = 5,050. Give the algorithm real memory and it collapses further: with M = 22 buffer blocks the outer relation is read in chunks of M − 2 = 20 blocks, costing ⌈100/20⌉ × 50 + 100 = 350 transfers. If either relation fits entirely in memory the cost falls to the best case b_r + b_s = 150. Indexed nested-loop join costs b_r + n_r × c, where c is the cost of one index lookup on the inner relation, and is the right choice when the outer relation is small and the join attribute is indexed. Merge join needs both inputs sorted on the join attribute and then costs one pass over each, b_r + b_s = 150; if they must be sorted first, add the external merge sort cost b_r(2⌈log_{M−1}(b_r/M)⌉ + 1), which for r with M = 22 is 300 transfers and for s is 150, making the sorted merge join 600 in total — still an order of magnitude below the tuple-level nested loop. Hash join partitions both relations on the join attribute and costs roughly 3(b_r + b_s), here 450, but works only for equi-joins and natural joins, whereas merge and nested-loop joins impose no such restriction.

How results move between operators is a separate cost decision. Under materialised evaluation each operator writes its intermediate result to a temporary relation on disk and the next operator reads it back, so a 500-block intermediate costs 500 transfers to write plus 500 to read — 1,000 extra block transfers that pipelined evaluation avoids entirely by handing tuples to the consumer as they are produced. Pipelining needs the consuming algorithm to accept tuples incrementally, which demand-driven iterators (open, next, close) provide; blocking operators such as sorting and the build phase of a hash join cannot be pipelined and force materialisation at that point.

Heuristic optimisation applies equivalence-preserving transformations without costing them, in a standard order. Break a conjunctive selection into a cascade of individual selections; push each selection as far down the tree as its attributes allow; perform the most restrictive selections first; replace a Cartesian product followed by a selection whose predicate joins the two relations with the corresponding join, because a join can use an index or a merge while a product cannot; push projections down so that only needed attributes flow upward, keeping join attributes alive until the join is done; and combine sequences of unary operations into one pass. Apply this to the canonical plan for a query over Student(rollno, name, deptid) with 20,000 tuples and Dept(deptid, dname) with 50 tuples of which one is Physics, written as π_name(σ_{dname='Physics' ∧ Student.deptid=Dept.deptid}(Student × Dept)). The predicate is a conjunction, so split it. The conjunct dname = 'Physics' mentions only Dept, so it pushes down to Dept and reduces it from 50 tuples to 1. The remaining conjunct mentions both relations, so it cannot be pushed below the product, but it is an equality across the two, so the product-plus-selection collapses into an equi-join on deptid. The intermediate that was going to be 20,000 × 50 = 1,000,000 tuples becomes 20,000 × 1 = 20,000. Note what is not correct: the selection on dname cannot be pushed onto Student, which has no dname attribute, and the projection on name cannot be pushed below the product because deptid is still needed to evaluate the join.

Cost-based optimisation goes further. Join order matters because join is associative and commutative, and the number of orderings grows factorially, so System R style optimisers restrict the search to left-deep trees and use dynamic programming, computing the best plan for each subset of relations once and reusing it, while tracking interesting sort orders that a later merge join could exploit. A rule-based or heuristic optimiser is cheaper but blind to data distribution; a cost-based one is only as good as its statistics. Exam shape: this leaf is small in the MCQ bank but every question in it is arithmetic, so the marks are entirely in knowing which formula belongs to which algorithm. In the conventional half it appears as 'given these relations and buffer size, compare the cost of three join strategies' or 'apply heuristic optimisation to this query tree and justify each transformation' — write the formula, substitute, and state the assumption about which relation is outer, because an unstated assumption is where the marks go.
facts: Query processing has three stages: parsing and translation into relational algebra, optimisation into an evaluation plan, and evaluation.
Simple nested-loop join costs n_r × b_s + b_r block transfers in the worst case; block nested-loop join costs b_r × b_s + b_r, and both fall to b_r + b_s when a relation fits in memory.
With M buffer blocks, block nested-loop join costs ⌈b_r/(M−2)⌉ × b_s + b_r, so 100-block r against 50-block s with M = 22 costs 350 transfers rather than 5,100.
For r of 100 blocks and s of 50 blocks, block nested-loop costs 5,100 transfers with r outer and 5,050 with s outer, so the smaller relation belongs on the outside.
Merge join on already sorted inputs costs b_r + b_s; external merge sort costs b_r(2⌈log_{M−1}(b_r/M)⌉ + 1) block transfers.
Hash join costs approximately 3(b_r + b_s) but applies only to equi-joins and natural joins.
Materialising an intermediate result of n blocks costs 2n extra block transfers — n to write and n to read — which pipelined evaluation avoids.
An equality selection σ_{A=v}(r) is estimated at n_r / V(A,r) tuples; a join on an attribute that is a key of s yields at most n_r tuples.
The core heuristics are: cascade conjunctive selections, push selections down, do the most restrictive first, convert a product plus a joining predicate into a join, and push projections down.
traps: Nested-loop versus block nested-loop is a single-word distinction with a fifty-fold cost difference: the tuple-level version multiplies by n_r (tuples of the outer relation) and the block version by b_r (blocks). Reading 'block nested-loop' and reaching for n_r × b_s is the standard lost mark.

A selection whose predicate mentions attributes of both relations cannot be pushed below their product, but it can still be absorbed into a join — options that say such a selection 'cannot be moved at all' confuse the two facts.
Materialisation costs both a write and a read of the intermediate, so a 500-block intermediate is 1,000 extra transfers, not 500.
Projections cannot be pushed below a join if they would discard the join attributes; pushing π down is only valid when every attribute needed by an operator above is retained.
Hash join and merge join are not universal substitutes: hash join handles only equality predicates, so a theta-join on an inequality falls back to a nested-loop variant regardless of cost.
mnem: Heuristics in one phrase: select early, project early, and never leave a Cartesian product where a join will do.

Database design, functional dependencies and normal forms

def: A transaction is a logical unit of database work that must satisfy atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability; a schedule is an ordering of the operations of several concurrent transactions that preserves each transaction's internal order, and recoverability classes constrain when a transaction may commit relative to the transactions whose uncommitted writes it has read.
exp:
The ACID properties are four separate guarantees delivered by different subsystems, and knowing which mechanism supplies which is what an applied question tests. Atomicity — all or nothing — is delivered by the recovery manager using the log. Consistency, that a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, is partly the application programmer's obligation and partly the constraint enforcement machinery. Isolation, that concurrent execution yields the same result as some serial execution, is delivered by the concurrency-control manager. Durability, that a committed change survives a crash, is delivered by write-ahead logging and stable storage.

A transaction passes through five states: active while executing, partially committed after its final operation but before its log records are on stable storage, committed once they are, failed when normal execution can no longer proceed, and aborted after rollback restores the prior state. The commit point is the moment the commit log record reaches stable storage, and it is the boundary that decides everything downstream. Before it, ROLLBACK undoes the transaction. After it, ROLLBACK is powerless — a committed transaction's effects are durable by definition — and returning the data to its earlier state requires a different facility altogether, such as Oracle's Flashback, which reconstructs a past state from undo or archived data rather than undoing an in-flight transaction. That distinction, rollback for uncommitted and flashback for committed, is a real exam question in this bank.

Recovery rests on the write-ahead logging rule: the log record describing a change must reach stable storage before the modified data block does, so that an undo is always possible. A log record has the form <Ti, X, old_value, new_value>, with <Ti start>, <Ti commit> and <Ti abort> markers. Under deferred modification the database is not touched until commit, so recovery needs redo only; under immediate modification, uncommitted changes may already be on disk, so recovery needs both undo for transactions without a commit record and redo for those with one. Checkpoints bound the work: at a checkpoint the buffers are flushed and a <checkpoint L> record written, and on restart the recovery manager scans backwards to the last checkpoint, building an undo-list of transactions active but not committed and a redo-list of those committed since, then undoes the first set and redoes the second.

A schedule interleaves operations from several transactions while preserving the relative order of each transaction's own operations. A serial schedule runs transactions one after another with no interleaving, and n transactions admit n! serial schedules — 3 transactions give 6. The number of possible schedules is much larger: two transactions with 2 and 3 operations admit 5!/(2!·3!) = 10 interleavings. Serial schedules are always correct but waste the disk and the CPU, so the goal is a non-serial schedule that is nonetheless equivalent to some serial one.

Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, address the same data item, and at least one of them is a write. So read-write, write-read and write-write conflict; read-read never does. A schedule is conflict-serialisable if swapping non-conflicting adjacent operations can transform it into a serial schedule, and the mechanical test is the precedence (serialisation) graph: one node per transaction, and an edge Ti → Tj whenever an operation of Ti precedes and conflicts with an operation of Tj. The schedule is conflict-serialisable if and only if the graph is acyclic, and any topological sort of an acyclic graph gives an equivalent serial order.

Work both directions. Take S = r1(X); w1(X); r2(X); w2(X); r3(Y); w1(Y). On X, w1(X) precedes r2(X) and w2(X), and r1(X) precedes w2(X), all giving the single edge T1 → T2. On Y, r3(Y) precedes w1(Y), giving T3 → T1. The graph T3 → T1 → T2 is acyclic, so S is conflict-serialisable and equivalent to the serial order T3, T1, T2 — even though S itself is not serial, since T1's last operation follows operations of both other transactions. Now take S' = r1(A); r2(B); w1(B); w2(A). Here r1(A) precedes the conflicting w2(A), giving T1 → T2, and r2(B) precedes the conflicting w1(B), giving T2 → T1. The cycle means S' is not conflict-serialisable, and no reordering will save it. View serialisability is a strictly weaker condition that additionally accepts some schedules containing blind writes; every conflict-serialisable schedule is view-serialisable but not the reverse, and testing view serialisability is NP-complete, which is why practical systems enforce conflict serialisability instead.

Recoverability is a separate axis from serialisability and the two are routinely confused. A schedule is recoverable if, whenever Tj reads a value written by Ti, Tj commits only after Ti commits. Consider w1(X); r2(X); w2(X); commit T1; commit T2. T2 performed a dirty read of X, yet the schedule is recoverable because T1 committed first — had T1 aborted after T2 committed, as in w1(X); r2(X); w2(X); commit T2; commit T1, the schedule would be non-recoverable, since a committed T2 cannot be undone and durability would be violated. The first schedule is recoverable but not cascadeless: it permits reading uncommitted data, so an abort of T1 before its commit would have forced T2 to roll back too, and that chain is cascading rollback. A cascadeless schedule forbids reading an item written by an uncommitted transaction, and a strict schedule forbids both reading and writing such an item until the writer commits or aborts, which makes undo trivially a restoration of the before-image. The containment is strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable, and each is a stronger discipline than the last with a matching cost in concurrency.

SQL's isolation levels are the standardised relaxations: read uncommitted permits dirty reads, read committed permits non-repeatable reads, repeatable read permits phantoms, and serializable permits none. Exam shape: only one bank MCQ sits on this leaf, but the conventional half examines it heavily, because 'test whether the given schedule is conflict-serialisable and give the equivalent serial order' and 'distinguish recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules with an example of each' are self-contained ten-mark questions. Draw the precedence graph in words — list the edges and where each comes from — and always state which conflict produced each edge rather than asserting the answer.
facts: Two operations conflict only if they are from different transactions, on the same item, and at least one is a write; read-read pairs never conflict.
A schedule is conflict-serialisable if and only if its precedence graph is acyclic, and a topological sort of that graph gives an equivalent serial order.
n transactions admit n! serial schedules; two transactions of 2 and 3 operations admit 5!/(2!·3!) = 10 possible schedules in total.
Every conflict-serialisable schedule is view-serialisable, but not conversely; testing view serialisability is NP-complete.
A recoverable schedule requires a transaction to commit only after every transaction whose written value it read has committed.
The containment is strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable: cascadeless forbids reading uncommitted data, strict forbids reading or writing it.
The write-ahead logging rule requires the log record for a change to reach stable storage before the modified data block does.
At restart the recovery manager scans back to the last checkpoint, undoing transactions with no commit record and redoing those with one.
Once a transaction has committed, ROLLBACK cannot revert its effects; restoring an earlier state requires a flashback-style facility instead.
traps: Serialisability and recoverability are independent properties. A schedule can be conflict-serialisable and non-recoverable, or recoverable and non-serialisable — proving one says nothing about the other.

Recoverable but not cascadeless is the distinction most often lost: recoverability only constrains the ORDER of commits, so a dirty read is permitted as long as the writer commits first. Cascadeless forbids the dirty read outright.
A non-serial schedule is not automatically incorrect — the test is whether the precedence graph is acyclic, not whether operations are interleaved.
Rollback versus flashback: 'the transaction was committed' in the stem rules ROLLBACK out entirely, so an option offering both is wrong.

An edge in the precedence graph is drawn per conflicting pair, not per operation; several conflicts between the same two transactions in the same direction still give one edge, but a conflict in the opposite direction creates a cycle.
mnem: Recoverability ladder R-C-S: Recoverable delays the commit, Cascadeless forbids the dirty read, Strict forbids the dirty read and the dirty write.
rel: Concurrency control, locking and time stamping
Database system concepts, architecture, interfaces and data independence

sub: Concurrency control, locking and time stamping
def: Concurrency control is the set of protocols that force interleaved transactions to produce a serialisable schedule; the pessimistic family does so with shared and exclusive locks disciplined by two-phase locking, and the optimistic family does so by assigning each transaction a timestamp and rejecting any operation that would contradict the resulting serialisation order.
exp:
Uncontrolled interleaving produces four named anomalies and it is worth being able to construct each. Lost update: T1 reads X = 100, T2 reads X = 100, T1 writes 150, T2 writes 120, and T1's increment has vanished. Dirty read (temporary update): T2 reads a value T1 wrote and T1 then aborts. Non-repeatable read: T1 reads X twice and gets different values because T2 wrote it in between. Incorrect summary (and its cousin, the phantom): an aggregating transaction reads some records before an update and some after. Concurrency control exists to make these impossible while still permitting more interleaving than a serial schedule would.

Locking is the pessimistic answer. A shared lock (S, read lock) permits other shared locks on the same item; an exclusive lock (X, write lock) permits nothing else at all, which is why the item under an exclusive lock is locked against access of any type. That is the entire compatibility matrix: S with S is compatible, S with X, X with S and X with X are not. Locks may be binary or shared/exclusive, implicit (held on a coarser item and inherited) or explicit (requested on the item itself). But locking alone does not guarantee correctness: a transaction that releases a lock and later acquires another can still produce a non-serialisable schedule.

Two-phase locking supplies the missing discipline. Every transaction has a growing phase in which it may acquire but not release locks, and a shrinking phase in which it may release but not acquire; the moment of its last acquisition is its lock point, and the theorem is that the transactions ordered by lock point give an equivalent serial order, so 2PL guarantees conflict serialisability. Concretely, a fund transfer written as lock-X(A); read(A); A := A − 50; write(A); lock-X(B); unlock(A); read(B); B := B + 50; write(B); unlock(B) obeys 2PL, because the only acquisition of B happens before the first release. Move unlock(A) one statement earlier, so that lock-X(B) follows a release, and the protocol is violated even though the same locks are taken on the same items — that single reordering is what 2PL questions are built on. The variants matter: basic 2PL guarantees serialisability only; strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit or abort, which additionally makes schedules cascadeless and recoverable and is what commercial systems implement; rigorous 2PL holds all locks, shared included, until commit; conservative (static) 2PL acquires every lock before the transaction starts and is the only deadlock-free variant, at the cost of needing the full lock set known in advance and of poor concurrency.

2PL's price is deadlock. A system is deadlocked when there exists a set of transactions such that every transaction in the set is waiting for another transaction in the set — that phrasing is the exam's own. Detection builds a wait-for graph with an edge Ti → Tj when Ti waits for a lock held by Tj, and declares deadlock when the graph has a cycle, resolving it by choosing a victim to roll back; the victim-selection rule must avoid always picking the same transaction, or starvation replaces deadlock. Prevention uses timestamps in one of two schemes that are easy to swap by mistake. Under wait-die, if the requester is older (smaller timestamp) than the lock holder it waits, and if it is younger it dies and restarts — a non-preemptive scheme. Under wound-wait, if the requester is older it wounds the holder, forcing that younger transaction to roll back, and if it is younger it waits — a preemptive scheme. Both favour older transactions, and both restart a rolled-back transaction with its original timestamp so that it eventually becomes the oldest and cannot starve. Timeouts are the crude third option. Lock granularity trades overhead against concurrency, and multiple-granularity locking makes a hierarchy of database, file, page and record workable by adding intention modes — IS, IX and SIX — that are set on ancestors top-down and released bottom-up, so a conflicting coarse-grained request can be detected without walking the whole subtree.

Timestamp ordering abandons locks entirely. Each transaction gets a unique timestamp TS(Ti) at start, from the system clock or a counter, and the protocol simply enforces that the schedule be equivalent to the serial order by increasing timestamp. Each data item X carries R-TS(X), the largest timestamp of any transaction that has read it, and W-TS(X), the timestamp of the transaction that last wrote it. When Ti issues read(X), the operation is rejected and Ti rolled back if TS(Ti) < W-TS(X), because Ti is trying to read a value that in the serial order has already been overwritten by a younger transaction; otherwise it proceeds and R-TS(X) becomes max(R-TS(X), TS(Ti)). When Ti issues write(X), it is rejected if TS(Ti) < R-TS(X), because a younger transaction has already read the value Ti is about to replace, and it is also rejected under the basic protocol if TS(Ti) < W-TS(X), because Ti's write is obsolete; otherwise it proceeds and W-TS(X) becomes TS(Ti). Work the case: let TS(T1) = 100 and TS(T2) = 200, and let T2 write X so that W-TS(X) = 200. If T1 now issues read(X), then 100 < 200 and the read is rejected — T1 is rolled back and restarted with a fresh, larger timestamp. If instead T1 issues write(X) while R-TS(X) is still 0, basic timestamp ordering also rejects it, but Thomas's write rule recognises that a write nobody will ever read is harmless and simply ignores the obsolete write, letting T1 continue. Thomas's write rule therefore accepts strictly more schedules than the basic protocol, and the extra ones are view-serialisable without being conflict-serialisable.

The trade-off between the two families is the point of the leaf. Timestamp ordering never makes a transaction wait, so it is deadlock-free by construction, but it pays with cascading rollbacks and possible starvation of a transaction that keeps being restarted; it is also not recoverable unless commits are deliberately delayed. Two-phase locking makes transactions wait, so it can deadlock, but it never rolls a transaction back spuriously. Multiversion schemes keep old versions of each item so that a read is never rejected or blocked, at the cost of storage and version maintenance. Optimistic (validation-based) concurrency control runs a transaction on private copies through a read phase, then a validation phase that checks for conflicts against transactions that committed meanwhile, then a write phase, and it is the right choice only when conflicts are genuinely rare, because its failure mode is a full re-execution. Exam shape: the MCQs on this leaf are definitional — the exclusive lock, the deadlock definition — but the conventional half asks you to apply 2PL to a given schedule and say whether it is legal, to build a wait-for graph, or to trace a timestamp-ordering protocol operation by operation stating for each whether it is allowed and how R-TS and W-TS change. Tabulating the timestamps as you go is what earns those marks.
facts: An exclusive lock excludes access of every kind; only shared-with-shared is compatible in the two-mode lock compatibility matrix.

Two-phase locking has a growing phase (acquire only) and a shrinking phase (release only); the last acquisition is the lock point, and ordering transactions by lock point gives the equivalent serial order.
2PL guarantees conflict serialisability but not freedom from deadlock; strict 2PL, which holds exclusive locks until commit, additionally guarantees cascadeless and recoverable schedules.
Conservative (static) 2PL acquires all locks before starting and is the only deadlock-free 2PL variant.
Deadlock is detected by a cycle in the wait-for graph, whose edge Ti → Tj means Ti is waiting for a lock held by Tj.

Under wait-die the older transaction waits and the younger dies; under wound-wait the older wounds the younger holder and the younger waits. Both favour older transactions and restart victims with their original timestamps.
In timestamp ordering, read(X) by Ti is rejected if TS(Ti) < W-TS(X), and write(X) is rejected if TS(Ti) < R-TS(X).
Thomas's write rule ignores rather than rejects a write with TS(Ti) < W-TS(X), accepting some view-serialisable schedules that are not conflict-serialisable.
Timestamp ordering is deadlock-free because no transaction ever waits, but it is vulnerable to starvation through repeated rollback.
Optimistic concurrency control runs in three phases — read, validation, write — and is suited only to low-conflict workloads.
traps: Wait-die versus wound-wait is inverted by half the candidates who see it. Anchor on the verb applied to the older transaction: in wait-DIE the older WAITS, in WOUND-wait the older WOUNDS. Wait-die is non-preemptive, wound-wait is preemptive.

2PL prevents non-serialisable schedules but does not prevent deadlock, and timestamp ordering prevents deadlock but does not prevent starvation — an option claiming either protocol solves both is wrong.
The two timestamp rejection tests are not symmetric: a read is checked against W-TS(X) and a write against R-TS(X). Checking a read against R-TS is the standard error.

Basic timestamp ordering rolls a transaction back when TS(Ti) < W-TS(X) on a write; Thomas's write rule discards that write instead and lets the transaction continue. Name which rule the question is using before you decide the operation's fate.

Implicit and explicit describe how a lock is obtained, not what it excludes; a question asking which lock blocks access of any type wants exclusive, not explicit, and the two words are placed together in the option list on purpose.
mnem: Wait-die: the older waits, the younger dies. Wound-wait: the older wounds, the younger waits. Either way the elder survives.
